models.name: Model A — Explicit Beam-Contact Deployment
models.what_it_computes: Time-resolved coil deployment into a compliant aneurysm surrogate using geometrically exact beam elements with frictional coil–coil and coil–wall contact to predict final intrasaccular geometry, packing density, and local contact area distribution.

models.name: Model B — Explicit Mass–Spring Surrogate
models.what_it_computes: Reduced-order explicit model representing the coil as a chained mass–spring–damper with penalty contact to estimate final deployed configuration, global packing density, and regional void fraction.

mechanisms.name: M1 — Deployment into a compliant sac
mechanisms.why_it_matters: The interaction between the advancing coil and a distensible aneurysm wall governs the achievable packing density immediately after placement.

mechanisms.name: M2 — Early post-deployment settling under cyclic pressurization
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Physiologic pulsatility can compact the coil bundle within minutes, altering packing density relative to the as-deployed state.

mechanisms.name: M3 — Contact friction heterogeneity due to nascent thrombus
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Spatial variation in surface friction at the sac wall and between coils can change how coils redistribute, affecting final voids and density.

deviation.detail: All credibility factors are scored on a 0–5 Evidence Strength Scale (ESS) for each model × mechanism pair, where higher values indicate stronger evidence.

expected_decision.outcome_source: The explicit beam–contact formulation provides decision-useful estimates of packing density immediately after placement and following early compaction, whereas the reduced-order surrogate supports rapid scenario screening with modest accuracy.
rationale_keywords: heterogeneous friction remains a dominant uncertainty

expected_context_of_use: The context of use is a preprocedural and intraprocedural computational aid that predicts final intrasaccular geometry, global packing density, and regional voids for a specified aneurysm sac shape, neck geometry, and wall distensibility, given a coil product line with known mechanical properties and surface chemistry.

findings.mechanism: M1 — Deployment into a compliant sac
spans: Round-trip energy error on a manufactured pendular coil benchmark, which exercises large rotations, curvature change, and repeated contact–separation cycles, remained below 0.7% for Model A and 1.9% for Model B across the stable timestep range used in production runs, indicating that integration and contact resolution errors were small compared with experimental scatter in density measurements.
The round-trip energy error benchmark exercised multiple contact pairs through ingress, looping, and withdrawal, and produced a 0.7% error at the production timestep of 0.9 microseconds.
findings.span: Round-trip energy error on a manufactured pendular coil benchmark, which exercises large rotations, curvature change, and repeated contact–separation cycles, remained below 0.7% for Model A and 1.9% for Model B across the stable timestep range used in production runs, indicating that integration and contact resolution errors were small compared with experimental scatter in density measurements.

findings.mechanism: M1 — Deployment into a compliant sac
spans: For M1, Model A’s predicted packing density matched micro-CT-derived values within an absolute mean error of 2.8 percentage points (95% limits of agreement 4.1 to +4.7 points).
Regional void fraction errors averaged 3.9 points across the dome, equator, and near-neck partitions.
findings.span: For M1, Model A’s predicted packing density matched micro-CT-derived values within an absolute mean error of 2.8 percentage points (95% limits of agreement 4.1 to +4.7 points).

findings.mechanism: M1 — Deployment into a compliant sac
spans: Environmental and procedural settings, including fluid tem-perature at 37 ± 0.2 °C, a heparinized glycerol–saline mixture with viscosity 3.2 mPa·s, inlet pressure oscillations cycling between 90 and 140 mmHg at 1.2 Hz, and catheter advancement speeds of 0.6–1.2 mm/s, were held within or bracketing clinical values and recorded with traceable calibrations to decouple physics errors from environmental mismatches.
The bench conditions reproduced 37 ± 0.2 °C fluid temperature, 3.2 mPa·s viscosity, and 90/140 mmHg pulsation at 1.2 Hz with traceable calibrations, and wall compliance within 0.6 kPa1 to 1.4 kPa1.
findings.span: Environmental and procedural settings, including fluid tem-perature at 37 ± 0.2 °C, a heparinized glycerol–saline mixture with viscosity 3.2 mPa·s, inlet pressure oscillations cycling between 90 and 140 mmHg at 1.2 Hz, and catheter advancement speeds of 0.6–1.2 mm/s, were held within or bracketing clinical values and recorded with traceable calibrations to decouple physics errors from environmental mismatches.
